blocks.prompt: The Bird That Sniffs for Its Dinner
blocks.text: Every bird you know has its nostrils up near its eyes. The kiwi is the only bird on Earth that does not. Its two nostrils sit at the very tip of its long beak, so the kiwi can push that beak deep into the forest floor and smell what is hiding down there. Most birds have a weak sense of smell and sharp eyes. The kiwi is the other way around. Its eyes are small and its sight is poor, but its nose is excellent, and stiff whiskers around its face help it feel its way through the dark. A kiwi does almost everything at night. It sleeps through the day in a burrow it digs with its strong legs. When the sun goes down it comes out to hunt worms, grubs, beetles, and spiders. Kiwi live only in New Zealand, and they cannot fly. Their wings are about as long as your finger and are buried under shaggy feathers that feel more like hair than like feathers. Their bones are heavy and full of marrow, not hollow and light like the bones of a flying bird. A kiwi is not built for the sky. It is built for the ground, in the dark, with its nose down.

blocks.prompt: A Bird Built Like a Mammal
blocks.text: Scientists sometimes joke that the kiwi is an honorary mammal. The joke has a point. A kiwi has no hollow flight bones; its bones are dense and filled with marrow, like yours. It has whiskers around its beak, the way a cat does. It digs a burrow and sleeps in it through the daylight. It hunts by smell in the dark. Its body temperature sits near 38 degrees Celsius, lower than almost any other bird and much closer to a mammal's. Its feathers have lost the neat zip-together structure that makes a wing work, so they hang loose and shaggy, more like fur. None of this is an accident. New Zealand spent millions of years with no land mammals in its forests except bats. The jobs a hedgehog or a badger might have taken were simply empty, and birds moved in. A flying bird that has nothing to escape from can afford to stop flying, and flight is expensive to build and to fuel. The kiwi's ancestors put that energy somewhere else: into legs, into a nose, into a night shift on the forest floor. There is one more oddity, and it is the strangest of all. The female lays an egg so large that it can weigh a fifth of her whole body. Inside that enormous egg the chick grows for about eleven weeks, far longer than most birds, and it hatches fully feathered, looking like a small copy of its parents. Nobody feeds it. Within a week or two it walks out of the burrow and starts sniffing for its own worms. Then people arrived, and brought stoats, cats, dogs, and rats with them. The kiwi's whole design assumes that nothing is hunting it on the ground. That assumption is now false, and it is the reason kiwi are in trouble.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.
The Egg That Should Not Fit
blocks.text: Hold a chicken egg in your hand. Now imagine an egg six times that size, laid by a bird barely larger than the chicken. That is a kiwi egg. Measured against the body that produces it, the kiwi lays one of the largest eggs of any bird alive: roughly twenty percent of the female's weight. An ostrich egg, which looks enormous sitting on a table, is only about two percent of its mother. In the final days before laying, the egg crowds the kiwi's insides so completely that she can barely eat, and she spends much of her time standing in cold water to take the weight off her feet. Why bother? The answer is inside the shell. A kiwi egg is unusually rich in yolk, and that yolk funds an extremely long development. The chick sits in there for around eleven or twelve weeks, while a robin manages the whole job in two. It hatches with a full coat of feathers and a working set of instincts, a miniature adult rather than a helpless pink beggar with its mouth open. No parent feeds it. It lives off the last of its yolk for the first few days, then walks out into the forest and begins sniffing for worms on its own. In the brown kiwi, incubation is mostly the father's work: he sits on the egg for those eleven weeks, slipping out of the burrow only to feed at night. For millions of years this was an excellent strategy. A chick that starts life large and capable does not need parents, and in a country with no ground predators, hatching small and helpless would not have mattered much anyway. Then stoats arrived. A stoat is a slim, ferocious hunter about the size of a rolled-up sock, and it was released in New Zealand in the 1880s to control rabbits. It found kiwi chicks instead. Where nothing is done to stop them, stoats and cats and dogs kill about ninety-five of every hundred kiwi chicks before those chicks are old enough to breed. The clever response is called Operation Nest Egg. Rangers lift eggs out of wild burrows, hatch them in safety, raise the chicks until each one weighs about a kilogram, and then carry them back to the forest. At that size a kiwi can kick hard enough to fight off a stoat. Survival for those chicks climbs from around five percent to about sixty-five. It is an odd kind of rescue. The egg was already the kiwi's answer to danger, an answer worked out over millions of years, and it was a good one. It is simply an answer to the wrong question now.

blocks.prompt: The Bird That Gave Up the Sky
blocks.text: A kiwi is a bird in roughly the way a whale is a mammal: technically obvious, visually confusing. It has feathers, a beak, and it lays eggs, and there the resemblance to the sparrow on your fence largely ends. It is about the size of a chicken. Its wings are three centimeters long, tipped with a small useless claw and buried so deep in its plumage that you cannot find them without going looking. It has no real tail. Its feathers have lost the tiny hooks that zip neighboring strands into a smooth flight surface, so each one hangs loose and the whole bird reads as furred rather than feathered. Its bones are dense and marrow-filled instead of hollow. It runs on thick legs that account for about a third of its body weight, and it cannot leave the ground at all. Its scientific name, Apteryx, simply means without wings. For a long time the story told about the kiwi was tidy. Kiwi belong to a group called the ratites, which also includes the ostrich of Africa, the emu of Australia, the rhea of South America, and the extinct moa of New Zealand. All are flightless. All live, or lived, on land that was once joined in the southern supercontinent Gondwana. The obvious conclusion was that one flightless ancestor had been carried apart on drifting continents, and the kiwi had simply ridden New Zealand away from its cousins. Ancient DNA broke that story. When researchers sequenced material from the extinct elephant bird of Madagascar, a creature that stood up to three meters tall and weighed as much as half a ton, they expected it to sit beside the ostrich, its nearest neighbor on the map. Instead the elephant bird turned out to be the kiwi's closest known relative. Two birds, one enormous and one the size of a football, on opposite sides of an ocean. The only way to explain that is that their shared ancestor could fly. Flight was not lost once, long ago, on a splitting continent. It was lost again and again, independently, by birds that flew somewhere safe and then discovered they no longer needed wings. New Zealand was exactly that kind of safe. Until people landed roughly 750 years ago, the islands held no land mammals except bats. Nothing hunted the forest floor by scent at night, and nothing hunted the animals that might. The job was open. The kiwi took it, and took it thoroughly. It moved its nostrils to the tip of its beak, the only bird known to have done so, and grew an unusually large olfactory region in its brain to process what those nostrils find. It grew whiskers. It let its body temperature settle near 38 degrees Celsius, several degrees below a typical bird, because it no longer needed the furnace that powers flight. It gave up much of its eyesight: kiwi have among the smallest eyes for their body size of any bird, and their genome shows the color vision genes quietly decaying, the way genes do when selection stops paying attention to them. Every one of those trades was a bargain for millions of years. Every one of them is now a liability. A ground-nesting bird that cannot fly, cannot see well, and has never had reason to fear anything with teeth is close to an ideal prey animal, and stoats have been in these forests since the 1880s. Without predator control, around ninety-five percent of kiwi chicks die before they are old enough to breed. The bird is on the coins, on the rugby shirts, and in the name New Zealanders use for themselves. It is also vanishing from the country it named, for reasons that have nothing to do with any flaw in the kiwi and everything to do with what came off the boats.
